Read this first · one minute

What this test tells us now

Dossier learns more from additional ratings in this controlled test. Its advantage over a simple recommendation method is small, and this test uses invented films.

Learning improves

After one rating, Dossier puts a liked film ahead of a disliked one in 53.9% of comparisons. After 40 ratings, it reaches 80.5%. Higher is better. The one-rating result is close to the 50% chance level, and only 27.8% of first-ten recommendation slots are filled.

The advantage is not established

After 20 ratings, Dossier scores 76.1%. The strongest simple method, similar film, scores 75.4%. The 0.7-point lead is too small to claim a reliable difference here. About 4.3 of 10 of Dossier's first ten picks are liked.

Corrections work unevenly

Dossier corrected 3 of 5 deliberately broad wrong guesses. In the other 2, it changed the guess but made its film ordering worse. Choosing its own rating questions improved ordering by only +0.7 points after 20 ratings, compared with random reasonable questions.

Some people remain poorly served

For the director fan, older-film fan, craft-first viewer cases, the 20-rating scores are 49.0%, 50.7%, 51.4%. Scores near 50% mean Dossier can barely distinguish liked from disliked films for these people.

Decision: Keep this as a repeatable check on the current code. Do not use it as evidence that Dossier works well with real films or viewers. The next test needs real film details and ratings that were recorded independently of Dossier.

The short answer

More ratings help. A simple method is still close.

After 20 ratings, Dossier puts a film this person likes ahead of one they dislike in about 76 of 100 comparisons. The best simple method, “Similar film,” scores 75.4%. Dossier leads by 0.7 points.

Among the first ten recommendations, Dossier finds about 4.3 of 10 liked films. The similar-film method finds 4.5 of 10. That is a more direct measure of what a person would see on the screen.

Dossier beats each person's strongest simple method for 2 of 18 people and loses for 14. We pick that strongest method after seeing the secret answers, so this is a demanding comparison rather than a method Dossier could use in practice.

How to read the main score: 50% is roughly random ordering; 100% means every liked film beats every disliked film. Higher is better because good matches appear earlier. 76.1% does not mean 76.1% of recommendations are liked.

What this test can say: It compares changes on the same made-up people and films. Names such as “Philosophical signal 4” identify one of 12 generated films in a category. They are test labels, not real film titles. This test cannot tell us how well Dossier works for real viewers. Two test people are still too predictable and reach an almost perfect score.
More ratings

Does Dossier improve as it gets to know someone?

Yes overall: the ordering score rises from 53.9% after one rating to 80.5% after 40. The chart compares Dossier with five simple ways to order films. Higher lines mean liked films are more often placed ahead of disliked films.

Early on, simpler methods can do better. At 20 ratings, Dossier narrowly leads on overall ordering. The similar-film method still puts more liked films in the first ten.

After 20 ratings, most test runs score between 50.0% and 98.8%. That wide range means some people get almost random results while others get nearly perfect ordering. The average hides those failures.

The test finds strong wrong guesses in 0 of 72 runs at 10 ratings and 8 of 72 at 40 ratings. Better recommendations do not guarantee that every stated belief is right.

Changing its mind

When an early guess is too broad, does Dossier let go?

For each case, Dossier first sees five ratings that support a broad guess. We then give it eight ratings that challenge that same guess. The person's unseen film ratings tell us whether the original guess was too broad.

In 3 of 5 cases, Dossier drops the tested broad guess without a large loss in film ordering. In 2, it changes its mind but becomes much worse at ordering unseen films. A better result would keep useful parts of the person's taste while dropping only the false generalisation.

The same ten films can remain on the recommendation list even when their order and the broader film ranking get worse. The score before and after tells us more than list overlap alone.

Choosing what to ask

Do Dossier's questions help it learn faster?

We start two copies of each person with the same five ratings. One copy rates films Dossier asks about. The other rates randomly selected, reasonably familiar films. We check both against the same secret films. A larger positive difference would mean Dossier needs fewer questions to learn the person.

After 20 ratings, Dossier's choices score 0.7 points higher than random choices. After 40 ratings, they score 1.2 points lower. These small and mixed results do not show a clear advantage for Dossier's question choice.

Total ratingsDossier chose next filmsReasonably familiar films chosen at random Difference for DossierRange of differences across runs
5 61.3% 61.3% no change +0.0 points to +0.0 points
10 62.9% 63.7% 0.9 points lower −13.1 points to +11.4 points
20 71.0% 70.3% 0.7 points higher −25.1 points to +28.8 points
40 75.1% 76.3% 1.2 points lower −24.2 points to +12.3 points

All percentages in this table mean “liked films ranked ahead of disliked films.” Higher is better. The two approaches start with identical first ratings.

A check on the test itself

Does the score fall when we give Dossier bad evidence?

Yes. We change the first 20 ratings in ways that should make learning harder. A large drop means the test notices bad input; if the score stayed the same, this benchmark would be suspect.

Flipping half the ratings lowers the ordering score by 25.6 points on average. Shuffling ratings among films lowers it by 32.7 points. More truthful evidence usually helps, though some individual people remain exceptions.

What we changedAverage drop in film orderingPeople who lost at least 5 pointsPeople with no clear drop
Flip half the ratings 25.6 points 14 of 18 3 of 18
Shuffle ratings among films 32.7 points 13 of 18 4 of 18
Remove the strongest ratings 22.1 points 14 of 18 4 of 18
Turn up to five likes into dislikes 25.2 points 14 of 18 3 of 18
Give only five ratings 20.5 points 12 of 18 5 of 18

A larger drop is good evidence that the test can tell useful ratings from misleading ones. It is bad news for a viewer who actually gives those misleading ratings.

The difficult people

Who would get the weakest recommendations?

These eight people have the lowest film-ordering scores after 20 ratings. Their cards show what Dossier saw, what the person really liked among the secret films, and which films Dossier placed badly. The possible reasons are explanations to investigate, not proven causes.

Director fan49.0% correct ordering

Loves films by one fictional director even when the films have little else in common.

After 20 ratings, Dossier put liked films ahead of disliked films in about 49 of 100 comparisons. That is close to random ordering.

Possible reason: Dossier notices some director evidence but still places many of this director's films near the bottom. This is a clue from this case, not a proven cause.

Simple comparison: Random order scored 52.9% for this person.

Checking the earlier test

Why did the first test look almost perfect?

One rating gave too much away

In the older, easier test, Dossier scored 98.0% after seeing just one liked film. A simple method that copied the taste clues from that one film scored 99.2% and also filled the first ten places with liked films.

That person and the secret films matched the same obvious style clues. The result showed that the test was too predictable. It did not show that Dossier understood a person after one rating.

Why the Avengers rating left the top ten unchanged

After a contrary rating for Avengers: Infinity War, Dossier kept one fewer taste guess. Its assessment of that film moved from -0.161 to -0.068, which is less negative. Dossier already had a rating for that film, so it left the film out of recommendations.

Other films' scores moved, but none crossed into or out of the first ten. A stable top-ten list alone therefore did not mean Dossier ignored the new rating.

The old test had 24 liked films among 48 secret films, and many films came from very similar groups. Even the simple one-film method got ten liked films in its first ten. The new test includes people whose preferences cut across those predictable groups.
What the results point to

Three things Dossier needs to do better

1 / Follow a taste across different films49.0%

For the director fan, film ordering is about as good as random. If this rose, Dossier would put more unseen films by the loved director ahead of unrelated dislikes.

2 / Ask more useful questions0.7 points higher

Dossier's chosen films barely improve learning over random reasonable films after 20 ratings. A larger gain would mean fewer ratings before good recommendations appear.

3 / Correct a guess without swinging too far2 of 5

In these cases, contrary ratings removed a broad guess but hurt film ordering by over five points. A better correction would preserve the person's genuine likes.

These are patterns in this test, not proof of which part of Dossier's code caused them.

What these numbers mean

How to read and trust this test

What Dossier did

The test uses 18 made-up people and 288 invented films. For each person, 216 films can supply ratings. Another 72 films stay secret until scoring. Each person likes at least five and dislikes at least five of the secret films.

Dossier receives only public film details and the ratings we choose to reveal. It never receives the person's hidden taste description, the secret ratings, or the extra rules used to make them. The test calls Dossier through the same CLI actions used outside the lab.

What “correct ordering” means

Take one secret film the person likes and one they dislike. Does Dossier put the liked film first? The score counts how often it does, with ties counting as half-right. The statistical name in the downloaded data is “AUC.” A score of 50% is chance; 100% is perfect.

Higher means better ordering. It does not tell you what share of the first ten films the person likes. “Liked films in first ten” answers that question. A run with no list scores zero in that column.

When Dossier returns no list, the test records 50% for film ordering. That means there was no ordering to judge; it does not count as a successful recommendation.

“First ten versus the best possible” also rewards putting the strongest likes near the top. It reaches 100% when those films appear in the best order. Higher is better for both first-ten measures.

What Dossier believes

A “strong wrong guess” has an internal strength score of at least 75%. The person's average rating for at least three matching secret films points the other way. Dossier's strength score is not a tested chance that the guess is right. Fewer wrong guesses are better.

The five change-of-mind trials choose early guesses that are too broad. At least four secret films, and at least 40% of matching secret films, contradict each guess. New ratings then challenge it. A correction counts only if Dossier changes the guess without making its film ordering much worse.

What the test cannot tell us

Dossier gives films an order, not a predicted personal star rating. That is why this report measures ordering and good films near the top instead of an error in predicted stars.

The numbered film names are placeholders. The generator made 24 categories with 12 films each so we could repeat the same test and control which film traits differ. Each film also has invented genre, keywords, director, series, and popularity. A name like “Animated wonder 2” identifies a test case; it does not refer to an actual film.

This design makes the result easier to reproduce, but it leaves out the messy differences between real films. Repeated categories may also make some tastes easier to learn. We invented the people too, and their preferences follow fixed rules about genre, director, series, endings, and craft. Two people still reach an almost perfect score after 20 ratings. Use this test to compare Dossier versions on these same cases. It does not predict results for real viewers or a real film catalogue.

We show each person's ratings in 4 different orders. For one person, a change under three points calls for closer inspection. It is not a decisive win or loss.

This HTML file contains the complete results and works without a server or internet connection.
